Hands-on Exercise 9b: Visualising Geospatial Point Data

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code

Author

JUNCHEN LI

Published

June 16, 2026

Modified

June 18, 2026

1 Overview

This hands-on exercise follows the learning flow of Chapter 22 from R for Visual Analytics. The teacher example focuses on visualising Singapore Pools outlets as geospatial point data. The main visualisation method is the proportional symbol map, where the size of each point symbol represents the magnitude of a numeric variable.

In this file, I first reproduce the teacher example. Then, in the Self Trying section, I extend the analysis by looking at high-winning outlets, zero-winning outlets, outlet type differences, and spatial concentration patterns.

2 Getting Started

2.1 Loading R packages

Code 
pacman::p_load(
  sf,
  tmap,
  tidyverse,
  DT
)

For this exercise, the sf package is used to handle simple feature data, tmap is used for thematic mapping, and tidyverse is used for data wrangling.

3 Teacher Example: Geospatial Data Wrangling

3.1 Importing Singapore Pools data

The code chunk below imports the Singapore Pools outlet data from a CSV file.

Code 
sgpools <- read_csv("data/aspatial/SGPools_svy21.csv")

sgpools

3.2 Checking the data structure

Before converting the table into a geospatial object, I inspect the field names and data types.

Code 
glimpse(sgpools)
Rows: 306
Columns: 7
$ NAME              <chr> "Livewire (Marina Bay Sands)", "Livewire (Resorts Wo…
$ ADDRESS           <chr> "2 Bayfront Avenue, #01-01 The Shoppes at Marina Bay…
$ POSTCODE          <dbl> 18972, 98138, 738078, 188306, 552542, 731001, 370064…
$ XCOORD            <dbl> 30841.56, 26703.87, 20117.93, 29776.95, 32238.69, 21…
$ YCOORD            <dbl> 29598.56, 26525.70, 44888.06, 31382.18, 39518.76, 46…
$ `OUTLET TYPE`     <chr> "Branch", "Branch", "Branch", "Branch", "Branch", "B…
$ `Gp1Gp2 Winnings` <dbl> 5, 11, 0, 44, 0, 3, 17, 16, 21, 25, 22, 25, 31, 27, …

The important fields are:

  • XCOORD: x-coordinate in SVY21 projected coordinate system
  • YCOORD: y-coordinate in SVY21 projected coordinate system
  • OUTLET TYPE: outlet category
  • Gp1Gp2 Winnings: number of Group 1 and Group 2 winnings

3.3 Creating a simple feature data frame

The data is currently an aspatial table. The code below converts it into an sf point feature data frame.

Code 
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(
  sgpools,
  coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
  crs = 3414
)

sgpools_sf

EPSG:3414 refers to the SVY21 / Singapore TM projected coordinate reference system. It is suitable for Singapore local mapping.

4 Teacher Example: Drawing Proportional Symbol Maps

4.1 Turning on interactive map mode

Code 
tmap_mode("view")

4.2 Basic interactive point symbol map

This first map simply shows the locations of Singapore Pools outlets and branches.

Code 
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "red",
    size = 1,
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  )

4.3 Proportional symbol map by winnings

The next map uses symbol size to represent the number of Group 1 and Group 2 winnings.

Code 
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "red",
    size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  )

4.4 Proportional symbol map with outlet type colour

This version improves the map by using colour to distinguish outlet types.

Code 
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
    size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  )

4.5 Faceted proportional symbol map

The teacher example also demonstrates that tmap view mode can work with faceted maps.

Code 
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
    size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  ) +
  tm_facets(
    by = "OUTLET TYPE",
    nrow = 1,
    sync = TRUE
  )

4.6 Returning to plot mode

Code 
tmap_mode("plot")

5 Self Trying: Exploring Winning Intensity of Singapore Pools Outlets

In this self-trying section, I use the same geospatial point data, but the analysis focus is different from the teacher example. Instead of only mapping all outlets, I try to identify where high-winning outlets are located and whether branches and outlets show different spatial patterns.

5.1 Preparing analysis variables

I first create several variables that make the analysis easier to read. I classify outlets into winning intensity groups and also identify whether an outlet has no Group 1 or Group 2 winnings.

Code 
sgpools_self <- sgpools_sf %>%
  mutate(
    winnings = `Gp1Gp2 Winnings`,
    win_status = if_else(winnings == 0, "No winnings", "At least one winning"),
    win_class = case_when(
      winnings == 0 ~ "0",
      winnings <= 10 ~ "1-10",
      winnings <= 25 ~ "11-25",
      winnings <= 50 ~ "26-50",
      TRUE ~ "Above 50"
    ),
    win_class = factor(
      win_class,
      levels = c("0", "1-10", "11-25", "26-50", "Above 50")
    )
  )

sgpools_self

5.2 Summary of outlet type and winnings

Before drawing the map, I summarise the number of outlets and winnings by outlet type.

Code 
outlet_summary <- sgpools_self %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(`OUTLET TYPE`) %>%
  summarise(
    outlets = n(),
    total_winnings = sum(winnings, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_winnings = mean(winnings, na.rm = TRUE),
    zero_winning_outlets = sum(winnings == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

outlet_summary
Code 
DT::datatable(
  outlet_summary,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  )
)

5.3 Bar chart of winnings by outlet type

This chart complements the map by comparing the total number of Group 1 and Group 2 winnings by outlet type.

Code 
outlet_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `OUTLET TYPE`, y = total_winnings, fill = `OUTLET TYPE`)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = total_winnings), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Group 1 and Group 2 Winnings by Outlet Type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total winnings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

5.4 Self Trying Map 1: Winning intensity map

This map uses both colour and size. Colour shows the winning intensity class, while symbol size represents the actual number of winnings.

Code 
tmap_mode("view")

win_palette <- c(
  "0" = "grey75",
  "1-10" = "#a6cee3",
  "11-25" = "#1f78b4",
  "26-50" = "#fb9a99",
  "Above 50" = "#e31a1c"
)

tm_shape(sgpools_self) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "win_class",
    size = "winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.6,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = win_palette),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winning class"),
    size.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winnings")
  )

5.5 Self Trying Map 2: High-winning outlets only

The next map focuses only on outlets with more than 50 winnings. This makes it easier to see where the strongest winning locations are located.

Code 
high_winning <- sgpools_self %>%
  filter(winnings > 50)

high_winning
Code 
tm_shape(high_winning) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
    size = "winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.8,
    size.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winnings"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Outlet type")
  )

5.6 Self Trying Map 3: Zero-winning versus winning outlets

This map compares outlets with no winnings and outlets with at least one winning. It helps to show whether zero-winning outlets are spatially concentrated or spread across Singapore.

Code 
tm_shape(sgpools_self) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "win_status",
    size = 0.7,
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.4,
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winning status")
  )

5.7 Faceted map by winning class

This small multiple map separates outlets by winning intensity. Compared with a single crowded map, the faceted version makes it easier to compare low-, medium-, and high-winning outlets.

Code 
tm_shape(sgpools_self) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "win_class",
    size = "winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.5,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = win_palette)
  ) +
  tm_facets(
    by = "win_class",
    nrow = 1,
    sync = TRUE
  )

5.8 Top 15 winning outlets

The table below lists the top 15 outlets by Group 1 and Group 2 winnings.

Code 
top15_winning <- sgpools_self %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(winnings)) %>%
  select(
    NAME,
    ADDRESS,
    POSTCODE,
    `OUTLET TYPE`,
    winnings,
    win_class
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

DT::datatable(
  top15_winning,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 15,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  )
)

5.9 Interpretation

From the self-trying maps, I can compare three aspects of the point data. First, the proportional symbol map shows that a small number of outlets have much higher winning counts than most outlets. Second, mapping only high-winning outlets reduces visual clutter and makes spatial concentration easier to observe. Third, comparing zero-winning and winning outlets shows whether low-performing outlets are randomly distributed or appear in certain areas. The faceted map further improves readability by separating outlets into different winning classes.

Code 
tmap_mode("plot")

## 1 Overview

This hands-on exercise follows the learning flow of Chapter 22 from *R for Visual Analytics*. The teacher example focuses on visualising Singapore Pools outlets as geospatial point data. The main visualisation method is the proportional symbol map, where the size of each point symbol represents the magnitude of a numeric variable.

In this file, I first reproduce the teacher example. Then, in the **Self Trying** section, I extend the analysis by looking at high-winning outlets, zero-winning outlets, outlet type differences, and spatial concentration patterns.

## 2 Getting Started

### 2.1 Loading R packages

```{r}
pacman::p_load(
  sf,
  tmap,
  tidyverse,
  DT
)
```

For this exercise, the `sf` package is used to handle simple feature data, `tmap` is used for thematic mapping, and `tidyverse` is used for data wrangling.

## 3 Teacher Example: Geospatial Data Wrangling

### 3.1 Importing Singapore Pools data

The code chunk below imports the Singapore Pools outlet data from a CSV file.

```{r}
sgpools <- read_csv("data/aspatial/SGPools_svy21.csv")

sgpools
```

### 3.2 Checking the data structure

Before converting the table into a geospatial object, I inspect the field names and data types.

```{r}
glimpse(sgpools)
```

The important fields are:

- `XCOORD`: x-coordinate in SVY21 projected coordinate system
- `YCOORD`: y-coordinate in SVY21 projected coordinate system
- `OUTLET TYPE`: outlet category
- `Gp1Gp2 Winnings`: number of Group 1 and Group 2 winnings

### 3.3 Creating a simple feature data frame

The data is currently an aspatial table. The code below converts it into an `sf` point feature data frame.

```{r}
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(
  sgpools,
  coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
  crs = 3414
)

sgpools_sf
```

EPSG:3414 refers to the SVY21 / Singapore TM projected coordinate reference system. It is suitable for Singapore local mapping.

### 3.4 Checking geometry information

```{r}
st_geometry_type(sgpools_sf)
st_crs(sgpools_sf)
st_bbox(sgpools_sf)
```

The output should show that the data is stored as point geometry.

## 4 Teacher Example: Drawing Proportional Symbol Maps

### 4.1 Turning on interactive map mode

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
```

### 4.2 Basic interactive point symbol map

This first map simply shows the locations of Singapore Pools outlets and branches.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "red",
    size = 1,
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  )
```

### 4.3 Proportional symbol map by winnings

The next map uses symbol size to represent the number of Group 1 and Group 2 winnings.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "red",
    size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  )
```

### 4.4 Proportional symbol map with outlet type colour

This version improves the map by using colour to distinguish outlet types.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
    size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  )
```

### 4.5 Faceted proportional symbol map

The teacher example also demonstrates that `tmap` view mode can work with faceted maps.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
    size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 1
  ) +
  tm_facets(
    by = "OUTLET TYPE",
    nrow = 1,
    sync = TRUE
  )
```

### 4.6 Returning to plot mode

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")
```


### 5.9 Interpretation

From the self-trying maps, I can compare three aspects of the point data. First, the proportional symbol map shows that a small number of outlets have much higher winning counts than most outlets. Second, mapping only high-winning outlets reduces visual clutter and makes spatial concentration easier to observe. Third, comparing zero-winning and winning outlets shows whether low-performing outlets are randomly distributed or appear in certain areas. The faceted map further improves readability by separating outlets into different winning classes.

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")
```
